title: What is known about 1RB0RA_0RC0LE_0LD1RA_1LB0RF_0LD1LC_1RD---
description: Proof status of the six-state BB(6) holdout 1RB0RA_0RC0LE_0LD1RA_1LB0RF_0LD1LC_1RD---.
intro: Nobody knows whether this six-state, two-symbol Turing machine halts when started on a blank tape: it is one of the holdouts left open by the bbchallenge project. This page lists what has been established about it, sorted by what each result rests on.
verdict: The question is open. The two basic counter increments (lowest digit 0, and lowest digits 1 then 0) are proved in Lean for all block lengths (kernel). The general increment rule matches all 2,282 clean increments of the first 3·107 steps, and the C simulator runs 2·1011 steps without a halt. Carries into the higher separators, the reservoir refills and the 1100 region are not yet rules.

claims.title: The halting configurations
claims.text: The machine stops exactly when it reads the symbol of a halting transition (F1); the generated statement covers every configuration.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10,000 steps
claims.text: The list simulator of the shared library, proved to agree with the machine's semantics, runs 10,000 steps from blank tape without a halt, evaluated by Lean's kernel.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps
claims.text: The same run, evaluated by compiled code.

claims.title: Increments for all block lengths
claims.text: From L 1 0 0 (1010)^(n+2) 0 0 (1010)^(m+2) 10 C> 0^∞ the lowest digit becomes 1, the lowest block gains four 10s and the reservoir loses two, in 24m + 12n + 122 steps (inc_d0); with lowest digits 1, 0 (L 1 0 0 (1010)^(a+2) 1 (1010)^(n+2) 0 0 …) both digits flip and both blocks gain two 10s, in 12a + 24m + 12n + 152 steps (inc_d1). half_sweep is the first of the two bounces.

claims.title: No halt in the first 2·10<sup>11</sup> steps
claims.text: The C simulator tmrun runs 2·1011 steps without a halt; the tape is then 391,889 cells wide. The shared cycle accelerator finds no cycle rules for this machine.

claims.title: The increment rule, checked
claims.text: Low 1-digits become 0, the next 0 becomes 1, its block and the lowest block gain two 10s each, the reservoir loses two. A direct simulation of 3·107 steps finds 2,282 increments that match and none that disagree; 141 carries run into higher separators and 17 reservoir refills fall outside the rule.

claims.title: A second region of 1100s
claims.text: Beyond the counter the machine builds runs of 1100 at the right end (half the tape at step 2·109) and later turns them back into reservoir 10s. Higher separators such as 1101, 0101, 000 appear between long blocks.

claims.title: Does it halt from blank tape?
claims.text: Not known. It halts exactly when C or E reads a 0 that has a 1 on its left and (10)^k 1 1 on its right. The increments never do this; the refills, long carries and the 1100 region are not closed rules yet.

explainer.lede: Nobody knows yet. This machine counts in binary on its tape, writing each digit as a single cell between long runs of 10, and pays for every count with cells from a reservoir. It has run 2·1011 steps without stopping.

facts.text: No halt in the C simulator.
The basic increments, proved for all block lengths.
Increments checked against the rule, none off.

sections.heading: The shape of the run
html: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape stopped growing in the second half of the run (bounded so far, or growing so slowly that no record fell in the last half). Right of the start it grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.507).
After 109 steps the tape spans 54,987 cells (20 left of the start, 40,988 right), with a density of 1s of 0.5.
These are measurements of one bounded run, sorted by tools/py/bbtools/triage.py; the macro structure behind them is the next thing to find.

sections.heading: What the tape is made of
html: Almost the whole tape is runs of the two-cell word 10 (accent colour). Between two runs there is a single extra cell, and that cell is a digit: …1 0 [0] 1 0… is a 0 and …1 0 [1] 1 0… is a 1 (orange). At the right end, after the lowest digit and its run, come a marker 0 0 and a reservoir of 10s (grey); the head is on the blank cell after it.

sections.heading: One increment
html: The head bounces twice between the right end and the low digits. The first bounce turns the marker 0 0 into 1 10 1; the second turns it back and adds one to the binary number read from the digits: the lowest 1s become 0, the next 0 becomes 1. The run after the digit where the carry stopped, and the lowest run, each get two more 10s; the reservoir gives up two.

Both are proved in Lean for every length of the runs. The general rule (any number of low 1s) is checked against the real machine for 2,282 increments.

sections.heading: A counter that pays for itself
html: The number stored in the digits goes up by one per increment, and the runs grow with it: run j gains two 10s every 2j increments, so the tape gets longer and each increment takes longer. The reservoir runs out regularly; the machine then refills it. Further right it also builds a second kind of region, made of the four-cell word 1100: at step 2·109 about half the tape is 1100s, and these are turned back into reservoir 10s later. High in the counter the separators are not always single cells (1101, 0101, 000 appear), a second layer of structure that the rules above do not cover.

sections.heading: Where it could halt
html: The only halting transition is F reading 1. Tracing back through D, the machine halts exactly when C or E stands on a 0 with a 1 on its left and (1 0)k 1 1 on its right: on this tape, inside a run of 10s that ends in a 1-digit. If the run ends in a 0-digit instead, the machine escapes into state B. The proved increments never do this; whether a refill, a long carry or the 1100 region ever does is the open part.

sections.heading: What is proved
html:
• Kernel: the increments half_sweep, inc_d0, inc_d1 for all run lengths (lean/Rules.lean); no halt in 10,000 steps.
  • native_decide: no halt in 107 steps.
  • Trusted computation: no halt in 2·1011 steps; the increment rule matches 2,282 increments.
  • Open: whether it ever halts.

family: binary counter with growing digit blocks and a reservoir
summary: A binary counter written in runs of 10s with one-cell digits; each increment spends two 10s of a reservoir at the right end and lengthens the blocks next to the carry; the basic increments are proved in Lean.
